title: How a Small Circle of Trump Allies Fast-Tracked a 250-Foot Arch on the National Mall
summary: A 250-foot-tall triumphal arch—topped with a golden Lady Liberty—could soon rise on Memorial Circle in Washington, D.C. But the path to approval has been anything but typical. An NPR investigation reveals that the project was conceived and pushed through by a small, interconnected group of classical design proponents close to President Trump, skirting the open competitions and public reviews that have governed memorials on the National Mall for over a century. The idea first surfaced in April 2025, when critic Catesby Leigh proposed an arch on a conservative think tank's website. His article included sketches by architect Nicolas Charbonneau of Harrison Design and by the National Monuments Foundation, led by Rodney Mims Cook, Jr. Months later, Trump appointed Cook to chair the Commission of Fine Arts—the very body that would vote on the arch. Cook did vote to approve it, despite the fact that the project had not undergone prior review by other stakeholders or Congress, as federal law requires. Charbonneau, meanwhile, posted his evolving designs on Instagram. By October 2025, Trump was showing donors models bearing Harrison Design's logo, joking about "small, medium, and large" options. At the April 2026 commission meeting, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum introduced Charbonneau as the lead designer. Cook sat with a "Make Design Great Again" hat on the table. Only one of the seven commissioners Trump appointed was a trained architect. Historians and landscape architects are alarmed. "We're seeing a complete avoidance of public review and public process that has underpinned this type of work since the Commission of Fine Arts was created in 1910," said Charles Birnbaum of The Cultural Landscape Foundation. The Washington Monument and Vietnam Veterans Memorial were both born from open competitions. Here, no such contest occurred. The National Park Service, which manages the federal land, is now processing permits. Critics argue that a handful of individuals with a shared aesthetic vision are reshaping the nation's most symbolic landscape without broad input.
why_it_matters: When a handful of insiders can fast-track a massive monument on the nation's most symbolic public space without wide input, it changes whose stories get told and how democratic our shared landmarks are. For young people, this case is a real-world lesson in how power, friendships, and political appointments can shape a city's—and a country's—identity.

background_read: The National Mall (the iconic park in Washington, D.C., that stretches from the Lincoln Memorial to the Capitol) has been protected by strict rules since the early 1900s, requiring open design competitions for major memorials. The Commission of Fine Arts (a federal body that reviews designs for public buildings and monuments in the capital) was created in 1910 to ensure aesthetic quality.

Rodney Mims Cook, Jr. (a classical architect and head of the National Monuments Foundation) is known for promoting traditional Greco-Roman styles in civic architecture. His foundation has been pushing for classical designs on federal land for years.

The Washington Monument and the Vietnam Veterans Memorial were both chosen through national open competitions, ensuring broad public input and diverse design ideas. None of that happened for this arch.

perspectives.description: Proponents argue that classical architecture embodies timeless values of beauty and triumph, honoring American greatness. They believe that the lengthy competition process has stifled bold, heroic designs and that this arch will inspire patriotism and tourism.

Critics charge that the project undermines a century of democratic tradition, ignoring the environmental, historical, and community voices that should weigh in on a federal memorial. They say a small clique with a shared aesthetic vision is imposing its taste without accountability.

The dispute reflects a deeper struggle between modern and classical design philosophies in public spaces, and the tension between expert review commissions and politically appointed leaders. The episode also tests existing laws that were designed to prevent exactly this kind of end-run around public process.

If this precedent stands, future memorials may be erected through private influence rather than open competition, allowing partisan symbols to dominate federal land. Legal challenges could delay the arch for years, and the controversy might spark new legislation requiring mandatory public review for any monument on the National Mall.
